utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in response to question 18 in your statement, you say that equal rights were afforded to everyone regardless of their nationality and, again, in response to question 44, regarding the SDS policy to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims or Croats, you say there were no policies of persecution, forced deportations or ethnic cleansing. Now, yesterday, we talked about co-ordinated attacks on neighbourhoods populated by non-Serbs but this morning I'd like to focus on the issue of forced deportations. Now, while you claim that there was no policy of forced transfer, it's true, isn't it, that in Sanski Most, as in other municipalities in the ARK, the position of the Serb authorities was that Muslims and Croats had to leave these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position was to treat everyone equally. However, if somebody takes up arms, organising secretly against the state, then that person loses that status. We have to distinguish between the policy of equal treatment for everyone and the relocation of population who wanted to join their own community, ethnic community; thus Serbs went from the parts where they were a minority in Bosnia-Herzegovina to parts where they were in the majority, and Croats chose to do the same, to feel safer. I know that several thousand Muslims spent months gathering various papers to meet all the requirements to depart. They had to have documents from various institutions of Republika Srpska in order to leave, and they had to have a permit from the area where they wanted to go, and a permit to cross the border. So the Muslims were organising to leave, and many of them are grateful to me to this day because I had helped them get their names on the lists for departure. So it was not expulsion, like I was expelled from Sanski Most. I was expelled from Sanski Most under fire, where they left in a civilised way with the escort provided by our armed forces. Of course, in all these situations, there were isolated cases and incidents, or, as you in the West would put it, collateral damage. But every such instance when a Serb inflicted pain on somebody else, is my pain, because I know that it was not the intention of the leadership of Republika Srpska to inflict pain on anyone and you can see that from the speeches of our presidents on many occasions, because Republika Srpska was established on St. Stephen's day and St. Stephen was a martyr for Christ.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Again, I remind you as I did yesterday to try and answer the questions as concisely and as precisely as possible and your answer to my question is, it was not expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to call up P3664.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, this is a 1st Krajina Corps command state of combat morale report, as you'll see, dated 14th of June, 1992, and it's from General Talic to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army Main Staff. I'm interested in page 2 of the B/C/S and page 4 -- excuse me, page 4 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. Sorry, perhaps it's the following page in the English. Thank you. And I'd like you -- to direct your attention to the last paragraph just before item 3 begins, and it states: The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of AOR Krajina, their security and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnia failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence. So, firstly, Mr. Tadic, this isn't about armed combatants, as you claimed. This is about Muslim and Croat refugees; and secondly -- well, can you comment on that? Do you agree that this document refers to refugees rather than armed combatants?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, you see a sentence here with the word "expulsion" and that's too strong a word for what was happening. I know only about Sanski Most. I cannot comment on other areas. I know there was huge pressure on the local authorities from people who wanted to leave and we couldn't even easily provide security, and provide them with the means to leave because it was difficult to organise it without incidents and deaths. And this reference to food supply, the situation was horrible then. The Serbs were being punished by the international community. Everything was blocked. Krajina was cut off. There was no food. There were huge shortages and we were all in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, it's clear from this document that Muslim and Croat refugees are being expelled and they do not want to leave. Now, you say you only know about the situation in Sanski Most. Let's refer to a document in which you discuss the situation in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3657.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the document that I'm calling up, Mr. Tadic, is one of the Executive Committee sessions which you stated yesterday that you attended, and at this session, there were extensive discussions regarding the forced displacement of Sanski Most's non-Serbs. You see that this is the minutes of and decisions taken during the 9th session of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most on the 27th of July, 1992. Could we please refer to English page 3 and B/C/S page 4. I'd like to focus your attention on item 4 which was the debate on the political and security situation on the territory of Sanski Most where Mirko Vrucinic gave an introductory presentation, and he stated that: About 4.500 Muslims and Croats have left this territory and continues that there are about -- there are still about 18.000 of them in our municipality. So Mr. Vrkes enters the discussion and he states: With respect to the political and security situation on the territory of the Sanski Most municipality, it has been rather unfavourable recently. There will be a joint meeting of the -- this is continued on page 5 of the B/C/S. He says: There will be a joint meeting of military and civilian authorities this week. A stumbling block for the new authorities was what to do with the other ethnic groups, Muslims and Croats. The most humane thing to do is to allow them to move away peacefully. Certain results have been achieved. We are working through UNPROFOR to resettle people who are interested in leaving the territory of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And he continues: We have to persist in this work because this is what the soldiers and the people of Sanski Most require of us because this has to be a Serbian town. So that was the true aim of the Sanski Most authorities, wasn't it, to ensure that Sanski Most was a Serbian town?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interpretation is lopsided. You see, in the contribution of Vlado Vrkes and the previous speakers, an exclusive position that it is also a request of the Muslims and their own wish to leave the territory, so their wish to leave coincided with the situation where providing enough food for the population and the aggravating crisis caused by sanctions imposed by the international community, and people needed a heap of documents from various institutions in order to be able to leave. And Vlado Vrkes - and you can even look at the previous speaker - says that Muslims are asking to leave and we need to make it possible for them in the safest possible way. That is separate from what was happening to the Serbs in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who couldn't even hope to leave in such a way, with safe escort provided by the authorities. We acted as a humane state, as humane people, to try to minimise casualties because war had been imposed on us, and once war begins, there are all sorts of evil happening. And if you go back to the previous speaker, he also talks about the fact that Muslims are demanding to leave. There was huge pressure on me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Muslims were asking to leave, weren't they, because of the conditions that we discussed yesterday, because of the massive destruction of their towns and because of the crimes being committed against them with impunity; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an exaggeration. It was the policy of the Muslim leadership, because in Trebinje nobody attacked Muslims, instead they had received orders to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we are not discussing Trebinje. And right now we are talking about the policy of your leadership and you noticed that -- or I'll refer you to your comment, which is halfway down the page, where you state how to implement the conclusions made here. And you say: To set up a council for people's defence and oblige someone from the higher commands to come to meetings so that all this can be implemented more efficiently. And before I ask you to comment on that, let's go to the conclusions that were being implemented. If we could go to page 8 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think it's fair to note that as the witness indicated, after passage related to 18.000 of them, Muslims, there is a sentence which goes to the effect that Muslims are asking to move away, and it should be made possible for them to do so, which you omitted reading. Having said that, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we refer to conclusion number 1 and three paragraphs down, it states: At present, about 18.000 Muslims and Croats remain on the territory of the Sanski Most municipality, and to avoid danger to the Serbian people, it is necessary to organise their voluntary resettlement. So here the Crisis Staff's conclusion is to organise the so-called voluntary resettlement of 18.000 Muslims and Croats, and your concern is how that could be implemented in the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm repeating again: War is an evil that Satan has imposed on the world, and in all that evil, we need to make sure to minimise it. It is evil when somebody has to leave their hearth, their home, but it's important to try to make the evil as small as possible. This is a very complex problem. You can't simplify. In the first point, there is a description of how difficult the situation is, militarily and politically. It's difficult to provide enough food for all the people, and if one part of the population wants to leave and the other, Serbian part, also wants them to leave, so as not to create more problems, to prevent the extremists on both sides to commit evil, and we wanted to enable the most humane possible resettlement, which is a necessary evil in all wars. You can see that all those Muslims returned before, and in Republika Srpska their property was restituted to them. But look at the situation of Serbs who had fled from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where did Serbs return? Did Serbs return perhaps to Kosovo? So all these consequences were to the detriment of the Serbs. Serbs are still leaving various areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why does the presence of Muslims, Croats, 18.000 of them, would cause danger to the Serbian people, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted to leave because in their ranks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you said that. But this document does not say because they want to leave, let them leave. It says, in order to avoid danger to Serbian people. Why do they cause danger to the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there were constant provocations. The weapons they had not yet surrendered, they kept secretly. There was always room for provocation, and our soldiers were not always under the control of their commands, and it was possible to create incidents that we didn't really need. And at the same time, their badgering of institutions in Sanski Most with demands to enable them to leave created huge pressure. We were snowed under their requests to leave, and we needed to enable them to do so with as little damage as possible, with as little -- few casualties and deaths. That was the situation, and through these conclusions, you can see that. We wanted them to leave in order to minimise the problems, and when their property was left behind, we never said that this property would now belong to the Serb refugee who had fled from the Federation of BH. We said it was property that was only in temporary use by someone else and we proved it after the war because that property was restituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether everybody's LiveNote is running.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If you reconnect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I had a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ver well, but it's running on the common computer. So shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I note that I'm out of time. There is one additional topic that I would like to cover briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in your capacity as head of the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska in Sanski Most, you were responsible for work obligation in the municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We are talking about a mobilisation all the resources including human resources and materiel resources for the functioning of the military, first and foremost, and also to improve the conditions of life under such harsh circumstances in Sanski Most; on the one hand, we had mobilisation for the army, and on the other, we had the work obligations because we had only few factories running but we had to keep them running in order to involve all those people who were not able bodied to allow them to survive. It was my task, the task of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, and my task as the chief of that department who was in charge of the municipality of Sanski Most. I attended the meetings of the Executive Council as a representative of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, as the chief of a department in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, as I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again, can we focus on the questions and give a concise answer. Your answer is: Yes, you were responsible for work obligation as the head of the Ministry of Defence in Sanski Most. But it's true, isn't it, that non-Serbs who were allowed to remain in Sanski Most were subjected to work obligation?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 25613.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tadic, this is a letter -- if we can in fact go to the signature page. Do you recognise your signature on this letter?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And this is your letter from the -- rather, to the Executive Board of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly regarding the work obligation units. If we could go -- my apologies. If we go to the first page, and you state: Over the past 16 months, the Ministry of Defence department of Sanski Most has deployed work obligations units consisting of non-Serbs as requested by the Army of Republika Srpska and various enterprises, institutions and individuals. You explain that work obligations were originally established -- rather, work obligation units were originally established in May 1993. And you state: Subsequently, units comprising non-Serbs began to be utilised while the units made up of Serbs never were. And if we could briefly go to the annex, please, which is the last page of the document, you'll see this details the breakdown of non-Serbs in work obligation in 1994 and you'll see it's in the region of 1.000 non-Serbs in work obligation. It's true, isn't it, that contrary to your testimony about the equal treatment of Serbs and non-Serbs, in the work obligation units that you were responsible for, only non-Serbs were required to do this labour; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, yet another lopsided opinion and a total misunderstanding of the situation. Let me tell you what this is all about. The Ministry of Defence engaged the most capable men for war operations for the military. Some of the population had to be deployed into work obligations. A report is only about that work obligation that the Muslims and the Croats had in order to give an overview of that, but the Serbs were also engaged in work obligation units. There are also tables that show you where they were engaged. Therefore, Muslims were in no way at all humiliated in that way. On the contrary, we involved them in the creation of new commodities and goods, we helped them to feel useful in the territory of Sanski Most, i.e., in Republika Srpska, and it is all explained so nicely here. The Ministry of Defence had a task to comply with requests of units, the Executive Council, and the factories. So whenever those institutions requested people, I would send them either Serbs or Croats or Muslims. This is the information about the engagement of Muslims and Croats only, which doesn't mean that Serbs did not have work obligation. Obviously we are talking about those who could not be deployed into regular military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure there is a translation issue, otherwise there's an omission. Can we go back to the first page of this document? Ms. McKenna read that sentence, probably you missed it, second paragraph, second sentence, I'll read from the first. Work obligation units were originally established in May 1993. And then second sentence reads like this: "Subsequently, units comprising non-Serbs began to be utilised while the units made up of Serbs never were." You state here that Serb units were not utilised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is a difference here. Before those units were set up for non-Serbs, we had work obligation for all the Serbs who were engaged on the same tasks in companies, in factories. However, we were faced with the military and security problem. There was a sentiment of insecurity, and the conditions were not ripe before them to set up those units. We feared incidents and problems because they had to be safe and secure. There was a war, fighting was going on, people were getting killed. The Ministry of Defence issued an order to set up those units. However, we always had to bear in mind that their use had to be made as safe as possible. This is the only difference. I repeat: Serbs already had work obligation in order to keep companies running, in order to be able to supply our units, in order to keep the war going on. Our priority, like in every war, were war activities and provisions for units engaged in the war, and deployed in the field. This order of the defence ministry means that Croats and Muslims should be made useful. They were not supposed to only sit at home but also to be made -- feel useful and involved in the life of society, although the society was a far cry from a normal peacetime society because there was war going on. But we tried to make sure that their engagement in war units did not compound the security situation even further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you talk about making Croats and Muslims feel useful and involved and as safe as possible in your work obligation units. An investigation took place into the war crimes committed in Sanski Most municipality in 1996, and the criminal report that was issued against you and other members of the Sanski Most authority detailed that during this work obligation, during the forced labour, that was carried out under your authority, non-Serbs were taken to the front line to dig trenches, carry ammunition and wounded, and many were killed in so doing. Non-Serbs were used as human shields and sent to minefields, and non-Serbs were subjected to physical and psychological torture. Now, that was the reality of the forced labour to which non-Serbs were subjected under your authority; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the table that you showed me just a while ago? I would like to use it to illustrate my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4 of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see here, this is a table with the exact breakdown of people from various places. You can see that there are 14 locations mentioned here with Muslims who were living there, and you see an overview of the work obligation places. It says local commune, military battlefield, military logistics, military wood chopping, socially owned enterprise. This is a table showing where Muslims were engaged in various work obligation units. My task, or our task, was to use the available population and to select those who were fit for various jobs and to send them wherever they were needed to perform those tasks from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sending them wherever they were needed included sending them to the front line and sending them to clear minefields and sending them to their deaths; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent many more Serbs to their deaths. This is about 113 people being sent to the front line. We, however, sent thousands upon thousands to the front lines. If I sent thousands of Serbs to the front line, why wouldn't I send a hundred Muslims to carry water, to dig trenches, and so on and so forth? Because we didn't consider Republika Srpska only a Serbian state. It does bear -- it does have the word Serb in its title, but we never thought that non-Serbs would not be living in our state. A state is as fortunate as it can afford rights and happiness to its minorities. Many more Serbs were killed by our enemies, and those were Croats and Muslims who were shooting at us. It is not only about the 113 who were sent to the front line to help the Serbian army in their activities. It was my task to mobilise people and to send them to those units or to other units, as you can see from the table. As I've already told you, Serbs were also engaged in work in privately and socially owned enterprises. Once conditions were in place, when the situation was safe, we could send Muslims to work there. Why would we send somebody to get killed if the situation was not safe? Obviously, those who inflicted harm on somebody else will have to answer God for that, not only courts. I had meetings with all those people. Not a single person was sent to the front line without me telling him with a lot of love that only hardships would await him there, and I did the same with the Serbs. But I thought that people had to help, that they had the obligation to help because a new Republika Srpska was being created. The previous state was broken up by people who hated, and we wanted to create our state from love. How could I be an aggressor on my own land? How could I be an aggressor in my own homeland of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would like to tender that exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That completes my cross-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God speed be with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please make a pause between my question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up P6541. I'm interested in page 1. Previous document. 6541.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Help us, Mr. Tadic, and tell us whether it is correct that this was issued on the 5th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we go to page 4 and look at the table again. Thank you. Mr. Tadic, what I can see here are 18 villages. It is true that -- is it true that on the 5th of October, 1994, you had 18 Muslim and Croat villages predominantly inhabited by Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is correct, and this tallies with the statement that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you not expel them already in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can see --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's questions are blatantly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about deportations, forcible deportations of the population. In October 1994, were these pure Muslim and Croat villages? Did the people remain living there?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They remained living there. It is correct that they were there. Those who did not want to leave were -- or if they requested subsequently to be allowed to leave, I organised meetings with them. They were never forced to be deployed to work obligation units. All those tasks were preceded by conversations where they were told what they were supposed to do and how they were supposed to do. I was sincere with those people and I tried to convince them that something new was being created, that no harm would befall them, and all that they could not accept that, they could not love us, they could still be convinced that I, as authority, would protect them. And they felt that on numerous occasions, I protected them, and not only myself, but also everybody else who constituted authorities in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what kind of obligations exist in wartime?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a war, priority was to mobilise people for war units. It was a very tall order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And second of all, there was work obligation for everybody, for Serbs and Muslims, to provide for the army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were Muslims duty-bound to join war units, to shoot and to fight?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Serbs? Were they duty-bound to join war units and to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were people paid in war units and in work obligation units?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a distinction made between the Serbs who were deployed in war -- work obligation units and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was better for the people, to be in a war unit or in a work obligation unit?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people were afraid of being killed or wounded. Many of the combatants asked me to transfer them to a work obligation unit, and when a healthy and able bodied person had to be transferred from a war obligation unit -- to a work obligation unit to a war unit, that was also difficult task. We protected Muslims and Croats from any bigger harm, at the same time allowing them to feel useful as a member of our society, as members of the state of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We no longer need this document. It's self-explanatory. Please bear with me for a moment. On page 4 of the previous document, P3657, mention is made of the pressures, and the document number is 3664, pressures on the government to allow Muslims to leave. Who was it who put the pressure to bear on the government?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit one thing to you. I have dozens of thank-you notes from people who thank me for my engagement in helping them to leave Sanski Most. They have been sending me such letters over the past years. Muslims and Croats wanted to leave the territory so badly that we sometimes could not meet their requests. However, we tried to make their departure as humane as possible with as few consequences as possible, because we were aware that we were creating a state that cannot persist on the evil and on crimes because every crime is a crime primarily for the human soul. And we all tried very hard, and that includes our President Karadzic, who is a believer and a good person. And you saw that yesterday that in Banja Luka, the first word he mentioned was democracy, which means that he is a person who, together with the Serbian Democratic Party, wanted to form a state that we would not be ashamed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw the minutes of a meeting, the document number was P3657, when Vrkes spoke. Was that recorded or was that just transcribed by the person who took the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was just transcribed by that person who took the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 101 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested to you, and it was read to you, that on the 28th people were first to jump and then they were killed. According to what you know, did the 6th Sana Brigade open fire on civilians and was the culture of attacking civilians being fostered by us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. That is a leading question and already the witness has made it clear that he didn't know anything about the incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Will you move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 99, it was suggested to you that there were prisoners and you agreed that there were indeed prisoners. The question contained the word "civilians." Were civilians detained in Sanski Most if they had not been involved in fighting?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two groups of people: Those who were detained after having acted against the army and against civilians, those were truly detained, true prisoners; and the second group involved transfer to a certain facility in order to avoid any major incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Vrhpolje and Tominska Palanka? Are they in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those settlements are not in Sanski Most. They are about 15 to 20 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Are they parts of the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Inappropriate question. Have you done with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have two or three more questions. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that unit break a law or did it violate the customs of war?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. Once again the same objection, it's totally inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness not say that he didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. When it comes to the transfer of the population from one village to another, he's aware of that and he said so. The Prosecution asked him about deportations. Now I'm asking him whether the removal of the population from one village is -- to another constitutes deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether a certain act is a violation of custom of war, I don't think it is for this witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, with all due respect, this witness was a representative of the Ministry of Defence in his municipality and he knew what was -- he knew the dos and don'ts and he is familiar with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 98, you were asked about events in the town itself concerning Mahala on the 27th of May, and you stated that you were not in town but in Palanka. What is the distance between Sanski Most and Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's show 65 ter document 04898. Could it be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please assist the witness to use the stylus to show Lusci Palanka and the route that you had to take through Muslim villages that you mentioned yesterday between Sanski Most and that place? A KDZ97 witness -- witness was KDZ97, under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the route you had to take to reach there?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be the 25 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please encircle the Muslim villages that you had to go through to get there?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tadic. Could you please place the date and your initials on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 97, it was suggested to you that 6th Sana Brigade took part in occupying the municipal building. Who occupied that building?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was occupied mainly by Muslims. I'm not sure how many Croats there were. They barricaded themselves in that municipal building, desiring to regain power from that building, power in the municipality of Sanski Most, although the SDS had won the elections in Sanski Most and, of course, they elected the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, or could you explain to the Chamber how was it possible for the war to start in Sarajevo on the 5th of April and in Sanski Most on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thanks to the arrival of the brigade and what I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it related to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That was my objection, Your Honour. It's outside the scope of the cross-examination, the start of the war in Sarajevo on the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, with all due respect, the Prosecution suggested that the Serbs attacked but war was preserved there for two months. I'm inquiring about a municipality where the Serbs are in power and there is 50/50 per cent of the population and I'm asking why didn't they attack right away and not two months later. It was suggested on page 97 that something happened on the 12th of July. Well, by the 12th of July, the work had flared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that arises from the line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown the publication, "Informator [phoen]," and you were told that this was a propaganda. What was the target audience of that publication?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to everybody, Serb population and everybody else, whoever could get hold of a copy could read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any propaganda in that publication? Did the contents contravene the facts?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may seem that the texts were harsh but this was nothing compared to what our ancestors had to go through and suffered a couple of decades earlier. I would like to tell the Chamber that the hardship that was imposed on us Serbs by the Germany -- by Germany and the fascists and the Ustashas was such -- such large scale that we had suffered atrocities which were not replicated in 1 per cent in the latest war. Five and a half thousand people were, on St. Elijah Day, killed and murdered. And in Jasenovac, which is a concentration camp that was never investigated properly, was the terminus point for thousands of people from Sana. And there were many more pursuant to German sources, and those wounds were still fresh. And in 1914, that very Serb people had to suffer such hardship. Fifty-six per cent of males in Serbia were killed in World War I. The only country whose army had to flee to another country, to Greece, to survive. Two great evils had been committed against the Serb people in the preceding century, and thank God for that brigade because that enabled us to maintain peace for an additional two months without suffering and without victims and sacrifice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tadic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Tadic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's probably best if we move into closed session, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could we move into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it the next witness is ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the next witness is Marko Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just wonder, I have a couple of points to raise with respect to the rendering of four adjudicated facts that the witness dealt with, pardon me, in his statement and I wonder if it might be better just to make those points before he comes into the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in -- this refers to adjudicated facts discussed in paragraphs 7, 17, 18 and 19. With respect, first of all, to paragraph 7, which deals with adjudicated fact 2433, I want to note that the version of the adjudicated fact discussed in the witness's statement deletes the location of Krasulje which is included in the original adjudicated fact. So it should read: Armed clashes broke out in Krasulje between local Muslims, and so forth. And the adjudicated fact referred to in paragraph 17, I, actually with respect to that fact, don't quite know what's going on, because the reference to 3500 houses which the witness discussed is -- appears in adjudicated fact 2448, not 2450.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And adjudicated fact 2450 reads completely different, I think. It says: Following the Crisis Staff's order, a Catholic church, at least four Muslim monuments in Kljuc, including the Atik mosque in the town of Kljuc, were either completely destroyed or heavily damaged by fire and explosives set by Serb forces. So I actually can't quite figure that one out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to adjudicated fact 514 in paragraph 18, adjudicated fact 514 also says something completely different. It reads: On 27 March 1992, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly established the Serbian MUP, and so forth and so on. And then with respect to 2428, finally, in paragraph 19, the version discussed by the witness does not include the first phrase in the original adjudicated fact, which is "in the days following 5 May 1992" these events happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may provide an answer, with your leave. Adjudicated facts are so composite and complicated as well as many questions put forward by the Prosecution. We do not deny that the MUP had been established, but it was stated there that non-Serb policemen were fired. Those facts are entwined in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's nothing to do with the objection raised by Ms. Edgerton. I'll deal with it when we discuss the admission of this statement. Very well. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Adamovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Adamovic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you for -- in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you as any other witness speaking Serbian to make a pause between questions and answers, and to proceed at a steady pace for everything to enter into the transcript. Did you give a statement to my Defence team, Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's please show 1D9595 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the last page to the witness so that he can see and identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today as you were asked by my associates, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement pursuant to the Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation as to the two paragraphs in which the adjudicated fact numbers were erroneously referred to, i.e., para 17 and para 18? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, first of all, I would like to apologise for that. As you know, the Prosecution filed a written pleading indicating that there were errors in the numbers of adjudicated facts and we directed our Case Manager to correct those errors but unfortunately, that job apparently wasn't done 100 per cent successfully. As far as the remedy, I think it's best to just leave -- this is a statement signed by the witness. I think it's best to just leave it in there. These adjudicated facts are referred to for the convenience of the Chamber in deciding whether they have been rebutted and don't constitute the evidence of the witness. The evidence is his answer. So we will inform the Chamber by e-mail of the correct adjudicated fact numbers, but I don't think there is any need to change the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your statement that they don't constitute the evidence of the witness. What did you mean, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, for example, if you look at number 17, which appears to be maybe a compilation of multiple adjudicated facts or a merging of them, the evidence is what the witness states and then he describes what happened during that period. So the fact that it's adjudicated fact number 2450 in the statement and it's really maybe adjudicated facts 2448 through 50, doesn't affect his evidence. Similarly for number 18, the reference to adjudicated fact number 514, the number is somehow different. It doesn't really affect his evidence as to what he explains happened with his contacts with his Muslim friends. So I think we can remedy it without altering the statement. But if you prefer us to alter the statement, we can do that. My only concern was whether that's a good thing to do after -- when the witness has already signed the statement like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would prefer the second option. I would like the Defence to redact those two paragraphs later on and -- and if the Defence wants to lead evidence as to this part, it should be led live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That wasn't actually one of the options that I had suggested, Mr. President. I was not talking about redacting the paragraph but changing the number of the adjudicated fact that's referred to. We don't have time to lead this evidence live and that seems to be an unnecessary penalty for a clerical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not a penalty, it's up to the Defence. And as to the remaining paragraphs, I think it will do no harm in admitting as it is with your caveat. Yes, the witness statement will be admitted into evidence. Shall we assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D4165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it there is no associated exhibits being tendered, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read in English a brief summary of Mr. Marko Adamovic's statement. [In English] Marko Adamovic worked at the Kljuc Territorial Defence Staff from 1976 until 1989. After that, he moved to the Kljuc municipality assembly to work on duties pertaining to Defence preparation in 1998 -- in 1989, and he stayed there until the start of the war in BH. The court of BH initiated criminal proceedings against him for war crimes in Kljuc, and in the first instance judgement he was acquitted of -- on all counts. Proceedings are currently ongoing before the appeal chamber. After the first incidents caused by the extremists, there was some chaos which lasted until the political authorities of Kljuc, the VRS and the civilian police were established. The roads were cut off, telephones were down and the security of citizens regardless of their affiliation and ethnic background was under threat. Individuals and groups wandered around the territory to acquire personal gain. When the Serbian authorities restored order, they also tried to establish peace and security for all people of Kljuc. Adamovic's unit, that is the Kljuc Battalion, received the task of controlling the territory with the goal of protecting all the people in the area. The unit carried out the task, treating every citizen professionally, humanely and honestly. In Velagici, there was a clash with the people who were found in possession of weapons and military equipment. Some of those persons who had been brought in tried to escape and the guards opened fire on them. The people who fired on the detained Muslims were arrested and proceedings were conducted against them. The grounds were not -- the guards were not members of either VRS or the police from Kljuc. During the clashes in the territory of Kljuc municipality, which lasted about 20 days, there was considerable destruction of material goods. As for the destruction of buildings, whether individual residential units or religious, this was not done by the army or police. During interventions and arrests of Muslim paramilitary units, the civilian population was called on to come out to an open space so that the legal military and police forces could see that they were not armed. The army shelled only the places where the armed extremists were hiding, and not populated areas. The political leadership of Kljuc municipality made an offer for all the people to stay in the area and live with the Serbs in peace. About 3.000 Muslims stayed to live in Kljuc in 1992/1993 and nobody mistreated them. Some Muslims joined the VRS voluntarily, and some joined the civilian police on a voluntary basis too. However, after the first incidents, all those who had someone in third countries tried to leave the municipality. This was true not only for the Muslims and Croats but also for the Serbs. The reasons to leave were primarily security, fear of war and fear of famine because the corridor was closed. Food and medicine supplies were low and there was no electricity or any other basic necessities for life. When a curfew was imposed it applied to all people and not only the Muslims. Everybody was free to choose whether to leave or stay, since the SDS of Kljuc municipality did not plan any ethnic cleansing of the non-Serbian population. The Red Cross helped people who voluntarily wanted to leave Kljuc and there was no need for any permit to be issued by the municipal authorities. The transport was organised privately or by companies and not by the police. Mr. Adamovic learned from his Muslim friends that the Muslim authorities had ordered them not to stay in any institution of Republika Srpska. In Pudin Han village, they formed the Muslim municipality of Kljuc together with the staff of units of the Territorial Defence. Furthermore, in all local communes where the majority of the population was Muslim, they issued a decision to secede from RS. In the whole territory of the municipality, there were joint check-points until May the 20th, 1992. They consisted of Serbs, Muslims and Croats and functioned until the Muslims left them following the instructions from their relevant organs from Sarajevo. And that is a short summary. At that moment, I would not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, since Dr. Karadzic read out in his summary that Adamovic was attached to a unit which was the Kljuc Battalion and that's not contained anywhere in the witness's written evidence, I would think Dr. Karadzic -- it would be incumbent upon Dr. Karadzic to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, I'm not sure I understood what the -- wherein the omission lay. Well, could you please tell us what was your connection with the battalion, the Kljuc Battalion, or with the Defence effort as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Kljuc Battalion was not the Kljuc Battalion. It was called so by the people. It was a battalion of the 30th Infantry Division which was deployed in the area of Mrkonjic Grad. We were summoned, called up, in the regular way and the battalion was established in the area of Sitnica. As I said, it was a part of the 1st Battalion Sipovo Jajce Brigade. It was past the 30th Division. I was assistant commander or deputy commander and assistant for morale and religious and legal issues. The 30th Infantry Division used the battalion as the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would that suffice? I thought that this was contained somewhere in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in its most part in writing; that is your written statement. And now you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But for now, we will have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we move very briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, I want to start by just asking you a little bit about the war crimes proceedings in front of the state court in Bosnia that Dr. Karadzic alluded to in his summary, and you refer to in your statement. Now, you said that these proceedings are presently before the appeals chamber. In fact, what happened in your case is after you were acquitted at the first instance, the matter went to appeal and the appeals chamber ordered you be retried; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that trial took place in March of this year, and the verdict hasn't been rendered yet, has it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the verdicts only -- they only expect the verdict to be rendered some time later this month, in fact, in December 2013; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So to be perfectly correct, you're actually still under indictment for charges relating to allegations of war crimes in Kljuc in 1992, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think I am a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Some of the offences that you were charged with include the killing of a number of people in Pudin Han around 28 May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll have a look at your indictment later. In fact, among the offences that you're charged with is included the killing of people in Prhovo on or around the 1st of June, 1992, and the killing of men, 77 men, at a school in Velagici on or around June the 1st, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These killings that I've just referred to, you're not denying they happened, are you? Because you actually confirmed in your statement that innocent civilians were killed in Prhovo and people were shot at Velagici while they were trying to scape. You're not denying them. They happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your position at your trial with respect to these offences was that when they happened, you weren't there; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the 27th of May, 1992, you said at your trial that you were in Mrkonjic Grad; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not concerning these events. I was not in Mrkonjic Grad when the killings in Velagici and Prhovo happened. I was in Kljuc at the time, but I was not on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At your trial, and Mr. Adamovic, I've listened to the transcript, I've listened to the trial as it was going on live and I heard you say that on 27 May 1992, you were in Mrkonjic Grad conducting reconnaissance. That's what you told the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that on the 27th of May, but you mentioned the 1st of June when the killings in Velagici and Prhovo happened. At that time, I was in Kljuc. However, on 27 May, I was in Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on the 10th of July, you were at Mrkonjic Grad as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, I was in Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the evidence you gave at your trial was that on the 1st of June, you were at a meeting of the Crisis Staff in Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, your position at your trial was that you weren't a member of the Crisis Staff but you attended their sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you went there to brief your immediate superior, your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. My brigade commander was present at the Crisis Staff and on the orders of my battalion commander I went to inform my commander on the situation in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also briefed your division commander, General Galic. You said that at your trial. You went to the Crisis Staff meetings and there you briefed your brigade commander and General Galic; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I briefed my commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Vukasevic, but I also stated that Galic was present at that meeting, once or twice, not every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, what you said at your trial was: With respect to the Crisis Staff every time I went there, there was the same group of people, and I note that I never went there without Lieutenant-Colonel Vukasevic or Galic being present. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. Perhaps he was absent a couple of times but after all this time I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these -- and you briefed them, these briefings, and their presence there was to make sure that everybody was on the same page, right, to make sure all the activity in the area was co-ordinated?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. I only know that I reported to my superior on the situation in the unit. Now, how the information I gave would be used by someone else, I didn't know then and I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And you briefed them often, you briefed them on a daily basis at that Crisis Staff, sometimes even twice a day; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it happened once that I briefed them twice in one day, but generally speaking, I informed not the Crisis Staff but my superior commander, and in that period, that was only five times. And twice I reported to my superior at the War Presidency because I was there only from 28 May until the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness said until the "20th June," not "28."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you don't know what the purpose of your briefing the Crisis Staff, your immediate superior, General Galic, during these Crisis Staff meetings would have been, I take it you're not a political man. You didn't pay any attention to what was going on during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was present at that meeting only the time it took me to do my duty and brief them, and then I left. There were sessions when I stayed on a bit longer, but, for the most part, I didn't stay until the end of the session while they were doing other things, dealing with other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And during your trial, you also gave evidence that until 1993, you were never a member of the SDS; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was president of the SK, the movement for Yugoslavia, at the level of the municipality south. That has been established through all my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you actually only joined the party so that you could keep your job; right? That was your evidence in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I said at the trial that I joined the party towards the end of 1993, and/or the beginning of 1994. A recommendation came down that assistant commanders for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs should be involved in the party; in other words, it was necessary for them to be members of the SDS. At that time I signed the paper joining the SDS and that, too, was established at the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so you weren't a member of the Crisis Staff, you weren't a member of the SDS and you also weren't a member of the War Presidency for Kljuc municipality, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like to clarify, we have problem with the negation in Serbian and in English. Sorry, in translation was that a no would be contrary to the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness confirmed that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff. Were you a member of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it clear to you, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, but in Serbian, translation was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I'd like to make it clear, what the Chamber ordered to redact from paragraph 17 and 18 from his statement is that the -- the reference to the adjudicated facts, so the part which appears after, "I can state the following" can remain in both paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I didn't understand it that way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So having put politics aside, let's talk about your military function. You explained to Dr. Karadzic that the Kljuc Battalion wasn't actually -- it was only called the Kljuc Battalion by the people and you said you were deployed in the area of Mrkonjic Grad. I'd like us to have a look at a document in that regard, please. It's 65 ter number 00895. So Mr. Adamovic, you've seen this document before, I know. It's dated 2nd November, 1993, and it's drafted by Slavko Culic, who succeeded Colonel Vukasevic as your brigade commander, and it's a supplement to the monograph of the first --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, no translation. So far I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you could repeat, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we are now talking about the Kljuc Battalion because you told Dr. Karadzic the Kljuc Battalion was only called that by the people and you said you were deployed in the area of Mrkonjic Grad. Now, you've seen this document before, Mr. Adamovic, and I'd like us to go over to page 3 in B/C/S and page 2 in English, please. Now, Mr. Adamovic, this document, this military report, specifically refers to the Kljuc Battalion as being formed on 18 April 1992, and lists you as its deputy commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Except, Your Honours, one needs to read this sentence till the end. The Kljuc Battalion which became part of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, as its 3rd Infantry Battalion, was stationed in the area of the village of Sitnica. It was called sometimes the Kljuc Battalion because all the members were from Kljuc. But, actually, it was part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. That's what I stated and that's how it was, and I was assistant commander of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's go over to page 3 in English and let's have a look at what the battalion was doing, and we can stay on the same page in B/C/S. This document says, Mr. Adamovic, when the armed conflict in Kljuc began, the entire battalion was relocated to the region outside Kljuc from where it was deployed to mop up the town and the surrounding settlements. The decision to assign this task - I'll just wait a second - to the battalion was issued on 27 May 1992. And the document lists the deployment areas of the 1st and 2nd Company. My question to you is: That's your battalion this passage is referring to; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The battalion's task was to disarm paramilitary formations and arrest them; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, I just saw that this was written by Lieutenant-Colonel Culic. Culic joined that brigade after several months of various actions in Kljuc. The battalion was not engaged in combat in Kljuc. The battalion was engaged only in controlling the territory from Pudin Han, Velagici, Ramici and Krasulje, controlling the road and all the movements in that area of the population, goods, et cetera. That was the task of the battalion. Why this commanding officer wrote this, I can't understand. The battalion was not employed in any other way, because other units did what it says here the battalion did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at this for a second. This document says the 1st Company of the battalion unit attacked from the area of the village Rezevici, the village of Hadzici, the village of Pudin Han. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. The company was only transferred there in the sector of Ramici. On the 27th there were no combat actions anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How would you know that when you said you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th, I arrived at Kljuc at night and the battalion could not have been without us, without the command. We came to Kljuc on the night of the 27th, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your trial on 27 May 1992, you were in Mrkonjic Grad conducting reconnaissance, was that also the truth?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in reconnaissance that morning and during the day, and we arrived at Kljuc around 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you go down further in the same document in English, last paragraph, and then go over to the next page in B/C/S, this document talks about the battalion's deployments the following day. The following day, it says: The battalion was deployed to carry out the same task in the area of the village of Pudin Han, Vukovo Selo, Humici, Plamenice, Vrhovo and Peci. A mopping-up operation in the villages of Kamicak and Vrhpolje ensued. That's true; right? That's your battalion.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is not true. It's not correct. And during my trial, we established and proved that the battalion was not involved in any combat operations. Why this commander who came later wrote this, including about some other battalions such as the Jajce and Sipovac Battalion, I can't understand. But during my trial, we proved undeniably, irrefutably that my battalion was not involved in these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Adamovic, we can go to the judgement in your first instance trial and see if what you said holds true because it's available on the internet and we'll do that later on. Let's leave this document aside for a minute, and leaving deployments aside for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to come back to it, but for the sake of reference why don't we just give it a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've talked about Crisis Staff meetings and meetings that you attended, and I'd like to have a look at minutes of meetings of the Kljuc Crisis Staff, that's P2606. These are meetings from May to July 1992. Now, you've seen this document before as well, Mr. Adamovic. So since you have --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Since you have, I'll go straight over to English page 10, B/C/S page 34, and that should show us minutes from the meeting of 3 June 1992. Could we just try the next page in B/C/S -- in B/C/S, please. It seems like every second page has this name and date stamp. Now, these minutes refer to your presence, Mr. Adamovic, at the meeting of June 3rd, and they describe you as the Kljuc defence commander and I want to show you another page. Let's go over to English page 17, B/C/S page 49, minutes of the 16th of July, 1992 -- pardon me, 16th of June, 1992. These minutes also describe you as defence commander. And we can actually even pop back over to minutes of the meetings of the 4th of June, if you'd like to see them, English pages 11 and 12 and B/C/S page 37. There, again, you're also described as defence commander. Now, you told this Chamber that you were never a commander of the Kljuc Battalion. We've seen, in the last document, P6543, you were actually a deputy commander. You've told this Chamber that you were a deputy commander for morale and religious affairs. That document we just saw, P6543, makes no mention of you having the position of deputy commander for morale and religious affairs. Instead, what we have here now, in June of 1992, is you noted by the Crisis Staff as being a defence commander, and that was defence commander for the city of Kljuc, wasn't it, Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It says in the minutes what it says but that was not the case, Your Honours. Please allow me to explain. I'll just need two sentences and I won't be long. On the 1st of June, the commander of the 30th Division came with an order to establish the command of town defence. He brought that order and in view of the situation on the ground - and let me not go into the details of what the town command was supposed to do - several officers had suggestions and proposals as to who that should be. According to one of the suggestions, I was supposed to be the commander of the town defence, but one session was not enough. The corps commander had to issue an order to appoint the town commander and the town command had to be established. I was told, orally, to prepare myself to become the town commander, but that lived for only three days. A subsequent order came to set up the 17th Light Infantry Brigade. Commander Drago Samardzija came and the setting up of the brigade started on the 6th of June. On the 1st of June, we received that first order to set up the town command. Those people who made those records, I don't know what to call them, they tended to call everybody commander. During those first days they called even me commander. However, the command of the town defence was never set up because, instead, the brigade was established, and I became the assistant commander of the brigade for moral guidance and legal and religious affairs. That was established during my trial, and that was how things indeed were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these minutes aren't accurate, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, the title is not correct. I can't talk about any minutes. I never took any minutes. What that person meant is entirely up to him.
