What I'm saying is this: The town command was never set up. There is not a single document corroborating the setting up of the town command. The town command didn't exist. Therefore, it did not issue a single order or a single document. I believe that you have that document talking about the setting up of the town command where it says the town commander will be, and then an empty dotted line, and the rest of the document, the dotted line was never filled out because the town commander was never appointed because he was supposed to be appointed by the commander of the 1st Corps. He was the person in charge of setting up all the commanders within the corps. Why he didn't appoint him, because four days later there was a change and the 17th Light Infantry Brigade was established. I became a member of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade on the 4th of June. You can see that in my personnel file. I'm sure that you can gain access to the personnel files of that brigade and you will find me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Adamovic, you just said there is not a single document corroborating the setting up of the town command. It's -- in fact, Mr. Adamovic, there is also not a single document corroborating your presence at the meeting of the Crisis Staff on 1st of June, 1992, is there? In fact, to the contrary, these minutes, and if we can go over in English to page 7, these minutes for the meeting on the 1st of June, 1992, don't list you among the participants. B/C/S page 27, please. Mr. Adamovic, you weren't there and you're grabbing at this as the only possible opportunity to alibi your presence at Prhovo on the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that this is only Madam Prosecutor's assumption, a mere assumption. The position of the town defence commander does not presuppose the command of a unit. If I was a town defence commander I would have never been in command of any unit. The town commander is never in charge of any unit, a smaller unit or a bigger unit for that matter. And if I had ever been supposed to be the town commander, I would not have been in Prhovo -- I could not appoint myself. You don't have those minutes but I have them. Are you not willing to show the minutes here? Or I can't say. But I have the minutes of the 1st where the town command was discussed and an order did arrive that the town command should be established. I was present. I don't know whether you have those minutes or not, but I have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, you're looking at them, and my question to you was: Mr. Adamovic, there is not a single document corroborating your presence at the meeting of the Crisis Staff. You have in front of you the minutes of the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the 1st of June, 1992. It's two pages. When the witness has had a look at the first page, we can flip over to the second page. You're not there.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to those minutes, I was not present. However, there were sometimes two or even three different sessions. I suppose that I was not there when those minutes were taken. However, in the course of that day, there were two or three sessions in view of the crisis. I attended that evening's session and I had arrived to inform the commander about the situation in the unit and then the proposal arrived to set up the town defence command. That document exists. It was issued on the 31st of May and it was presented at the meeting in Kljuc on the 1st of June. Why the second set of minutes is not there, I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. You haven't got a single piece of paper to corroborate your presence at a Crisis Staff meeting on the 1st of June, 1992, have you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I stated that I had that paper. It is not here, I don't know why, but I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What do you have, Mr. Adamovic? And you knew you were coming today, you knew you were coming for a long time ahead of time. Mr. Adamovic, are you saying that you have evidence that confirms your presence at this meeting on the 1st of June, 1992, and you didn't bring it? Mr. Adamovic, you didn't bring it at your own trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina either, did you, because it doesn't exist?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I had that document -- I didn't bring it myself because the Prosecutor showed it to the Trial Chamber, and it is in the file of that case, but I did not know that I was coming here to be questioned as a suspect, and you are now questioning me as if I were accused. That's why I don't have it. I am here to testify and in my testimony I'm supposed to follow the statement that I provided, and now you're not sticking to that statement at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I want to know what you have. Do you have a set of minutes that records you as being present at a Crisis Staff meeting on the 1st of June, 1992, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A set of minutes that shows that the command of the defence of the town of Kljuc was set up on the 1st of June, and I have those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over to the next page in B/C/S and in English, please. Mr. Adamovic, it's not here, and you didn't offer those minutes at your trial in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You never said they existed. That's because it never happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, you're going to have to skip over to the odd-numbered pages. I really apologise for forgetting about this. And I don't know why in B/C/S these copy certifications are uploaded as separate pages. Thank you. Oh, now, wait a minute. It seems like the B/C/S is -- the B/C/S doesn't correspond with the English translation page. In all fairness, let me have a look at that, please. Do you know what? The B/C/S pages, even though they are uploaded in the way in which they are stamped with an ERN are out of order. And in fairness to the witness, I'm not going to deal with this any more until he can get a chance to look at the correct version and I'm just going to move on, and we'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to stay, Mr. Adamovic, on the subject of the take-over of Prhovo on the 1st of June, 1992, and the killings during the take-over. Mr. Adamovic, when you said in your statement that the state court in Bosnia acquitted you of any responsibility related to the event, you actually omitted to say that they found that you were there the day before the attack. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was there every single day in the sector where things were happening, not only in Prhovo but in all of the surrounding villages, because I lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's correct, you were in Prhovo the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not correct. And I never said that. The day before the attack, I was not in Prhovo. There were witnesses who said that they saw me. Allegedly, I was wearing a uniform, the others said that I had a camouflage uniform, some saw me in civilian T-shirts, but I'm sure I was not in Prhovo. It was established by the Court who was there and who carried out those activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The day before the attack on Prhovo, at paragraph 304 of their judgement, the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina accepted witness testimonies and concluded that you were present when soldiers mistreated the residents of Prhovo on the day before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was not there, absolutely not. And it was proven, contrary to the testimonies, that on that day I attended the meeting of the Crisis Staff. On that day, the order arrived to set up the town defence command. During my trial, it was established which units had done it and which units had been deployed in the area. During my trial, I was forced to say the name, but the Prosecutor there did not want to accept my suggestion. She stuck closely to the indictment and she tried her hardest that I was there. I was never in command of a military police unit, and there was a military police unit there. And I told the Trial Chamber, You have a VOBH, she found mine, she could find the VOBH of the military police officers who were there. She could have listened to the testimonies of a couple of people who were -- who would have corroborated the fact that those military policemen were indeed there. She could have done all that instead of trying to pin guilt on an innocent person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talked about -- well, what you actually said about those testimonies of people who put you in Prhovo, either the day before or the day of the attack, was that they were lying and that you thought that it was all pre-arranged. Those lies, you thought, were all prepared in advance. That's what you said in your trial at the state court; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Adamovic, it's not those witnesses, it's not just those witnesses who testified in your trial at the state court who placed you in Prhovo the day before and the day of the attack. It's a large number of additional witnesses. Let's have a look -- just talking about the 30th of May, 1992, let's have a look at 65 ter number 25732. Mr. Adamovic, this is a statement to this Tribunal taken in 1997 from Nafa Krantic, and she talks about Serb soldiers passing through her village, which was Plamenica, on 28 or 29 May, 1992. If we could go over to the next page, please. I'm going to read this to you because I don't think you speak English or read English. But what Ms. Krantic says: On Saturday, either 28 or 29 May, 1992, Serbian soldiers entered our village. They came as infantry and then one APC. They wore regular JNA uniforms. And then she goes on and she talks about what -- their feelings of fear, that the soldiers told them that nothing would happen and to stay in the village. And she says: The commander was the teacher, Marko Adamovic, whom I know. He was teaching me in the elementary school in Humici. That day he wore a JNA uniform and I saw he had some rank on his epaulettes. That day I only recognised Marko Adamovic and the soldiers passed through the village. Mr. Adamovic, this woman, who didn't testify in your trial, recognised you as her teacher and she recognised you in the immediate area of Prhovo on 28 or 29 May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: And what am I now supposed to say? I claim that she did not recognise me because she did not see me there. Your Honours, during my trial, there was a witness who was born in 1971, and I taught school until 1972, claimed that I was a teacher, that he knew me, that he knew that I was a teacher, and he had never seen me before, never. Twelve years later, he claimed that he recognised Marko Adamovic's words on the bull-horn. Let's start from the initial assumption. If you know military structure, you will know that Marko Adamovic could not be in charge of Pragas, APCs and anything else. It would be impossible. But nobody prevents her from telling whatever she wants to say and it's not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were a teacher in Humici before the war, weren't with you, before you joined the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, until 1973, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. In fact, Mr. Adamovic, there is not one, there is not two, there is not three, but there is -- and this is just dealing with the day before the attack, there is multiple witnesses who gave evidence to this Tribunal about events in Prhovo on the 1st of June, 1992, and each one reports seeing you there, and these are not witnesses, Mr. Adamovic, who testified at your trial. Let's look at 65 ter number 25733. It's a statement to this Tribunal taken in 1997, so five years only after the incident, from Bajro Hadzic. He didn't testify at your trial, and if you go over to page 3, if you go over to page 3, the second full paragraph, he describes the 1st of June, 1992, the occupation of Prhovo by soldiers. He describes people being called out through a loud speaker. He describes seeing Marko Adamovic, who had the command. I know Marko Adamovic. He was working in the military department in Kljuc. He was a captain in the reserves, and in Humici, he was teaching children. So you've conceded you were a teacher in Humici. You were also -- it's true, isn't it, you were also a captain in the military reserves; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was a teacher, and I stopped teaching and joined the TO staff, and I was a member of the reserves, and I'm not saying that people don't know me. I'm just saying that I was not in Prhovo on the day when those activities happened. It is well-known which unit was there, which unit was deployed in the area, and Marko Adamovic was not in command of that unit. I have no other answers, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We are going to look at one more document, 65 ter number 25738. It's the ICTY statement of a survivor from Prhovo by the name of Azim Medanovic taken in 1997. Now, if we go over to page 4, he says, about halfway down the page: "Of all the Serbs there in Prhovo on the 1st of June, 1992, I recognised only Marko Adamovic. He wasn't masked, it was obvious he was in charge. I remembered him from the time when he was a teacher in Peci. I'm not sure I would recognise him now, but I did at the time." And further on on this same page, Mr. Medanovic describes being separated from the women and children in Prhovo, being marched out of the village in a column. He describes you taking a microphone, ordering women and children to be killed, and the village burned to the ground. In the column, this witness says you ordered it was -- it be split in two. This witness says you beat him. This witness describes how five people who couldn't stand up after being beaten were killed. He describes how a soldier singled out a 16-year-old from the column and shot him after you called out that there were too many of them. And he was saved, this witness, when one of his prospective executioners recognised him. Mr. Adamovic, these people have lost family, friends. They have been beaten. They have been threatened. They have been detained. You're still indicted, though. These witnesses have no interest in telling anything but the truth. It's in your interest, still under indictment, to exculpate yourself from the charges you faced in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, fully consciously, I state with all moral and other responsibility, that I did not carry out those actions that the witnesses are mentioning. Nobody is prohibited from saying what they think or any other information -- or to share any other information. It was proven at trial because there was this activity, it was known who was involved, there is a written order - maybe you, lady, don't know that - by the commander of the 1st Corps specifying which unit was supposed to go there. And I'm reiterating this was a platoon of the military police from Banja Luka, from the 1st Krajina Corps. It went there to control the territory. At the exit of Prhovo village, they were caught in an ambush by a paramilitary armed group who opened fire at a column, killed some civilians, and then there was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you weren't there, how do you know so much about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not finish, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Adamovic --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: And that is when the conflict --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- answer my question, please. If you weren't there, how do you know enough to give us this explanation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was about to explain. I know about these things because the officer in question at the meeting concerning the establishment of the town defence command, that officer came in, and I have witnesses from the Crisis Staff members who attended -- the members attended the meeting saw that officer who came in crying. He said that I was there with Pragas and APCs, we were ambushed, one member of the military was killed, and Prosecution witnesses confirmed that, and then after that, that soldier was killed, there was spontaneous fire being opened, quite a lot of people were killed, he was crying, and he asked for some people to be sent there to expect what was -- what had been done to the civilians. In my defence, I don't want to be responsible for somebody others' actions, Your Honours. I stated the name of that officer and stated the -- which unit was involved there. And if this is not true, I offer my head on the block. I wanted to help the prosecution to blame those responsible, but they didn't want to. They wanted to frame me. But truth will out eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Adamovic, you said you had witnesses from the Crisis Staff who could talk about this story. I'm going to just read you the evidence of one of the Crisis Staff members, Mr. Rajko Kalabic, and I apologise if I mispronounce it, that he came to testify before a Chamber of this Tribunal in the case against Brdjanin. And he talked about the events in Prhovo on the 1st of June, 1992, at transcript pages 22664 and 22665. He said nothing about someone coming into the meeting afterwards and upset about what had happened in Prhovo. In fact, he said: It was only after the event that the information reached the Crisis Staff, whether it was on the same day or one or two days after the events, I can't say. So the Crisis Staff member who came to testify here in defence of Mr. Brdjanin says something completely different to you. The truth is: You were there, and it's only in your interest to deny it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Rajko Kalabic testified in my trial as well and corroborated what I'm saying, and some other members of the Crisis Staff as well. Maybe he wasn't asked about that in that other trial. Maybe at that time he did not know what was going on after so many years, but he did testify in my trial, and he corroborated the words that I'm offering to you here and now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, so you're saying that Mr. Kalabic gave different evidence at your trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina than what he gave on the same subject as a defence witness here at this Tribunal? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that he did testify that on that day I did attend the meeting of the Crisis Staff and that I wasn't in Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different subject. I want to just touch on some of the incidents that you discussed in paragraph 3 of your statement, under the heading, "Paramilitary and para police organisation incidents in Kljuc." Now, all of those incidents -- and you've got a copy of your statement in front of you so you look at paragraph 3. All of those incidents happened on the 27th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those that I mentioned. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And all those incidents that you refer to happened at a time when Serb authorities were in total control of Kljuc municipality, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Kljuc was controlled by two, not just the Serbian authorities, but also the Muslim authorities. On the 27th, the municipality was split into two territories, that under the Serbian authorities and that under the Muslim authorities, because they seceded --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, these incidents happened in areas that were under the control of Serbian authorities at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Those incidents took place in the area controlled by the Muslim forces. In Velagici, Ramici and Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, given your answers I want to show you a document. It's P3438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical difficulty with e-court. Shall we break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a somewhat early lunch break. We will resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We left off trying to have a look at P3438, if my colleague could bring that up on the screen. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, what you see in front of you are minutes of the 8th meeting of the Kljuc Crisis Staff on 23 April 1992. And at this meeting, in the third paragraph under point 1, on the page in front of us, you see Veljko Kondic, who is president of the SDS municipal board, say: "Serbs are the majority population in Kljuc. We control all the important positions." Actually, I think in B/C/S it might be on page 2. Yes. I think so. So Kondic says: "Serbs are in the majority in Kljuc. We control all the important positions." And if we go over to page 2 in English, and page 3 in B/C/S, paragraph 2, you see Mirko Rosic say -- he tells people at the meeting, at the Crisis Staff meeting: The SUP is ours. And there is nothing to divide. So, Mr. Adamovic, we left talking about -- we broke off before lunch talking about Serb authorities being in total control of Kljuc municipality, and it doesn't take a politician to figure out that what Kondic is saying is that by the end of April, all power in Kljuc was controlled by the Serbs. That's what Kondic and Rosic are saying, isn't it? All power in Kljuc is controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in those party political meetings. I was not there. And I personally, my opinion is, if you wish to hear it, is that most of the authority in the territory of Kljuc was in the hands of the Serbs. But in mid-May, there was a splitting up of the municipality into two parts, and that territory which was predominantly populated by the Muslims was -- was under the control of the Muslim leadership, MBO and the SDA, and they separated the Pudin Han, Velagici, Krasulje, Filipovici and other villages, that area predominantly populated by the Muslims split off from the municipality. They issued decisions on that split, and, for that reason, I believe that they controlled that particular territory. They formed municipal staff of the TO, units of the TO, and they armed people, controlled the territory, set up check-points, facilities, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you took them back; right? You took those places. Pudin Han, Velagici, Krasulje and other villages, you took them back; right? That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Kljuc did not retake those villages. I see this differently. I see this from a military point of view. After the ambush at -- of the line of young soldiers departing from Zadar towards Serbia, which was ambushed in Kljuc, there was a double ambush in Velagici and Pudin Han by the Muslims. They attacked six or seven young soldiers. Nineteen were injured. The 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps units intervened there and those units took that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're repeating your statement and that wastes time. You've taken all that time to say to us that the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps intervened and those units took that area, so what I put to you was right. You took it back; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I answered you that this wasn't done by the civilian and other organs of the Kljuc municipality. These were military organs. My purpose when answering was to express that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at what the civilian authorities of Kljuc municipality did. I'd like to get out D1724, please. It's a public announcement from the Kljuc Crisis Staff, Mr. Adamovic, and it's dated 8 May 1992, so it's a little over a week after the document we just looked at. And this document informs the public that since the 7th of May, 1992, the police in the whole municipality are going to be wearing blue berets with the Serbian flag and that from this point forward, a Serb flag would fly from the Kljuc municipality building, signifying the fact that Kljuc municipality is now a part of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, Mr. Adamovic, what the -- what the -- what the authorities did is, on the 7th of May, 1992, they put into effect a unilateral political and military take-over of control of the municipality, and all aspects of life in it. That's what this document shows. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot comment on this public announcement. I did not take part in forming that decision. I wasn't there. At that time I was with my unit 20 kilometres away, and I cannot comment or be responsible for the activities or for the consequences stemming from this public announcement or this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on. Now, we looked earlier on today at a document that's now got the number P6543, and it was a supplement to the monograph related to the 1 KK, and you said, with respect to that document, that it was effectively a fabrication by the man who came to be your brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We could have it up just so the witness remembers what he gave that comment on. P6543.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what you said, when we talked in terms of this document about military operations by your battalion, was that you couldn't understand why the brigade commander wrote it; right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at P5406, then, please. This -- you would recognise this sort of a document. This is a daily combat report from the command of the 1st Infantry Brigade - and we can go over to the second page and Mr. Adamovic can see who signed it - to the command of the 30th Infantry Division. See, it's got the typewritten signature of Milorad Vukasevic. That's your commander. Now, we can go back to the first page in both languages, bullet point 2, and have a look at bullet point 2, the second-to-last paragraph of bullet point 2. Sorry, I've got my numbering wrong. I apologise. The second-to-last paragraph of bullet point 2 is on the second page in English. Could you go to page 2 in English? My apologies. There we go. That paragraph says, I think you have to do the same in B/C/S, but I'll read it for Mr. Adamovic. It says: Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion was -- of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims don't surrender their weapons by 27 May 1992 at noon, the battalion will carry out a mopping-up operation. And to this battalion, Combat Group 2 has been attached and has been under our command since last night. That's your battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander, I don't know about this document. I wasn't battalion commander. This, as you know, is addressed to battalion commanders, such documents as this. He could tell you more about that. I couldn't. I wasn't the commander. I didn't even know it existed. Brigade commander issues orders to battalion commanders, assistant commanders for moral guidance do not command battalions. I cannot comment on this document. I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you said you didn't know why P6 -- why your commander at the time wrote P6543, why that monograph was written, why it had those deployments set out in it. What this document you're just looking at shows you, Mr. Adamovic, is that the monograph or the supplement to the monograph was written that way because it's true. This document confirms exactly what was written in P6543, in terms of the deployment of your battalion, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stated that it was unclear to me why battalion commander, who subsequently came to that post after Vukasevic, wrote this. For this reason, at that time, the battalion could not have been issued with a combat task. We had not been equipped, no ammunition, was not trained for that. The battalion was rather deployed to control the territory between Pudin Han and Krasulje, inclusive of both villages, and this was where the battalion was deployed on the 29th or the 30th and it did -- it would stay put, it would carry out control of territory operations, and sometime around 20th of June, that battalion went to Jajce as part of the Tactical Group 2 and carried out activities in the territory of Mrkonjic Grad municipality. What I do know and what I do state is that my battalion - I had left by that time - never committed any evil acts in the areas where it held control. I can say before this forum that the citizens of Krasulje, Ramici, cried when the battalion set off towards Jajce because they thought who would guarantee them safety after they are gone?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is -- we are getting off topic. Let's stick with this time period. You talked in your answer about the 29th and 30th of May, and said that your battalion was deployed to control the territory between Pudin Han and Krasulje, and I'd like to have a look at 65 ter 25725, please. And we'll look at what your battalion was doing on the 30th of May. This is a combat report from the command of the 1st Infantry Brigade Sipovo command to the 30th Infantry Division and it's dated on 30 May 1992. So we need to go over to page 2 in both languages, please, and I want to look at the second-to-last subparagraph of bullet point 2. That says, in the Velagici, Kula, Pudin Han area, the 3rd Battalion is conducting mopping up of Green Berets who are surrendering in droves. Some of the Green Berets have fled and are in hiding. One of our soldiers was killed. Mr. Adamovic, they weren't controlling the area. They were clearing the area out of non-Serbs, and that's what this document shows. What you're saying isn't true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say non-Serb population, it says Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Clearing the area of Green Berets. What you said your battalion was doing is completely untrue and that's what this document shows. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is not the case. I state that the battalion did not carry out any mopping-up operations. I can bring you 300 witnesses to testify to that. The battalion was transferred through that area and was tasked with controlling the road in the area of Pudin Han, et cetera. But the mopping up operations were carried out by other units but not mopping-up operations. They were after a sabotage group that had carried out an attack in the area of Busija and this was done by units of 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the 3rd Battalion did no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we've looked at three separate military reports from the 3rd Battalion. You're saying all of them are lies. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: My evidence is that the battalion did not participate in these combat activities. It participated in controlling the territory. That's what I maintain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence, despite what this document says, your evidence is that the battalion was not involved in mopping up; right? It was not involved in mopping up the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Had nothing to do with clearing the area of non-Serbs, despite what these three documents say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection again. Again non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honours, I'm entitled to put our case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that would mean that your battalion was lying in their reports to General Galic and General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't maintain that he was lying. You should ask perhaps the author, the commander, why he wrote that. Maybe initially he did get that task but I know that that task was not executed, and the battalion did not mop up the terrain from Green Berets as it says there, in the municipality of Kljuc. It simply wasn't involved in combat activities one single day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you weren't there, so on what basis can you possibly deny the veracity and the accuracy of these reports? Your evidence is you weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, which date is it, in the order?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you -- you've read it. You know that it's the 30th of May. You've said you weren't there. You've said you weren't there at any of these critical moments. You said that you were not in Prhovo on the 30th of May. You said you were not in Pudin Han on the 30th of May. So on what basis are you saying that these documents, these military reports, are untrue?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I wasn't there. I was part of the battalion on the 30th of May. I didn't say I wasn't there. I was a member of the battalion. But the battalion was active on the axis Pudin Han-Sanski Most, et cetera. And the battalion was not involved in the Pumici [phoen]-Plamenica-Prhovo axis or in the mopping up of the terrain, and from that trial in Sarajevo, my trial, it was possible to make that finding, I believe the Trial Chamber made that finding, and made the judgement as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I tender this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P6544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on to another area, Mr. Adamovic, you talked in paragraph 11 of your statement about the killings at Velagici and you said that 12 members of the unit responsible were arrested and proceedings conducted against them. So when you say the unit responsible, members of the unit responsible, you're referring to the VRS soldiers who were responsible for the killing of these prisoners at Velagici; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not right. In my statement, I said that units from the territory of Kljuc, or the units of the VRS, were not responsible. It was JNA units which were in that area and were moving from Croatia that stayed in Laniste and were responsible. Twelve of their members perpetrated what they perpetrated. The authorities of Kljuc immediately arrested these men. The responsible judicial authority, and I don't know who else, conducted an on-site investigation, the perpetrators were arrested, judged and sent to serve their sentence in Banja Luka. And that's why I said that the authorities had done their job, as best they could. They made the arrests, but it was not VRS members or members of the units from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, clearly, Mr. Adamovic, when you said in your statement that you didn't know any of the details, that was absolutely correct because what happened was that those VRS soldiers responsible were arrested a couple of days after the killing. They were released from custody. An investigation -- they were still out of custody in March of 1993 when the first request for investigation into the incident was launched. By August -- pardon me, by July -- July 29th, 1993, more than a year after that killing took place, only two of the 12 VRS soldiers responsible were in custody and their detention was terminated after one month. And, Mr. Adamovic, on 29 July, 1993, the military prosecutor's office of the 1st Krajina Corps command proposed to halt any proceedings against these 12 people and the Court followed that recommendation. The proceedings never happened, they were judicially halted, there was no intention to bring them to justice, and you've just told us a lie, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I refer to P3614, 6143 and 3616 with respect to the evidence I've just cited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond. First of all, I don't agree with what Madam Prosecutor just said. In my statement I only stated things that I know. I don't know about everything that happened. And I shouldn't be told that I'm lying. I only stated what I know, and I stated that in that sector, there was a unit in transit that was responsible for these acts. I don't know about everything that happened, but I know the authorities reacted and made arrests and sent these people to the competent institution. An on-site investigation was conducted, and I believe the authorities of Kljuc did their job properly. As to what later happened with those soldiers, whether they went to the 1st or the 2nd Corps or before a military court, I don't know. I have no clue about these things. And I believe that I'm not lying. I am telling only what I know and that's all I said in my statement, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on to another topic, you said in your statement that -- and it was in, I think, paragraph 6 -- that 3.000 Muslims stayed to live with the Serbs in Kljuc in 1992 and 1993. But, in fact, more than 15.000 Muslims left, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, but the point of my statement was to say that three and a half thousand Muslims who wanted to stay stayed, that there was no expulsion, because I was asked what I knew about the expulsion of the Muslim people. I know that our authorities did not persecute Muslims, did not expel them. Those who were arrested, disarmed and who were responsible for some offences, they were expelled; whereas, normal, peaceful Muslim people who wanted to live there were able to go on living there. And I also want to say that politics got involved. People were being talked into leaving. I have lots of friends in many circles. I have very good friends among the people who left. There was a lot of political pressure. There was also much fear, chaos, panic. And lots of people fled Kljuc, not only Muslims but also Serbs who feared joining the army, who feared crisis, war, God knows what else. That's all I wanted to say in my statement. That's the only point I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very few, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you, Mr. Adamovic, to explain to us this last thing you said? Which people did you mean when you said that politics got involved? Who from the politics?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Muslims. The SDA and HVO exerted pressure on people to move to other territories where Muslims were in the majority, and that was the area of Bihac, Zenica, Tuzla, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we please look at P02606, minutes of Crisis Staff meetings. You said you were mentioned as the town commander. Who else was mentioned as town commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, it was Bosko Lukic, major; Major Dusan Petrovic; Major Branko Ribic; and Marko Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of educational attainment did the recording secretaries on the Crisis Staff have?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the cross-examination whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, we have to establish whether they put the correct names on various speakers. Could we see page 21 in B/C/S? I'll have to see the English page. No, sorry, page -- one page before, 29 May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: While we are getting that, Mr. President, I don't understand myself how when the Prosecution is relying on the accuracy of the minutes of the Crisis Staff, how that question could not arise from the cross-examination when the accuracy of those minutes can be challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Educational attainment? I don't see where it's going, even if we have any evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think where it's going is calling into question whether or not these minutes are accurate, but that seems to me to be within the scope of the cross-examination which was what the objection was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to -- very well, let's hear the evidence. The witness answered the question but we didn't hear the translation. Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's not quite clear to me which question should I answer? Could the question be repeated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said who kept these minutes at the sessions of the Crisis Staff? What kind of education did these people have? Were the meetings recorded or were the notes taken by hand?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not recorded. There was no electricity, not even for lighting to see properly what you're writing, let alone for recording. It was some young clerks who took these notes. I don't know whether the officials of the Crisis Staff took any notes themselves, because I attended these Crisis Staff meetings only for five, ten minutes. I would come, inform my commander about the situation in my unit, he would then release me, and what they did after I left, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at this session of 29 May, item 2? Could you read item 2 out loud? Item 2.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That a defence command be set up and Major Bosko Lukic be appointed as its commander. Until then he was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: "The Crisis Staff is continually in session. It is monitoring all developments in the territory of the municipality because combat operations are underway and information from the ground is coming in."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it mean, "is continually in session"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That means that the Crisis Staff is constantly at the office with all of its members, and, occasionally, when they find a spare moment, they have lunch and some rest, but most of the time they are in their offices and busy working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do all the people who come to a particular meeting come on time and stay until the end of the meeting, or are people coming and going all the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe most of them stayed throughout the session, but sometimes people had to leave early because among them there would be doctors and businessmen and people in different types of industry whose other engagements required their attention elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we need the next page, and leave the same page in English. Could you look at item 4?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the public security station reported to the staff negative events on the ground which reflect adversely on the entire situation and are linked primarily to theft, breaking and entering, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you look at the entry for 30th May? I believe it's page 21. Yes. It's page 21 in B/C/S. Could you tell us, what is it at the bottom, considering that there is information?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That their armed forces are in Plamenica village and have no intention of surrendering --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I help? Force them by using force, the Crisis Staff needs to make sure, to the extent possible, to avoid all arson, looting, et cetera. How does this fit in? Is it consistent with what you know about the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the Crisis Staff only tried to preserve security and to create favourable conditions for a normal life for all the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't see you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Keeping in mind that the witness has already given evidence that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff, and at temporary transcript page 40, that he was only present at -- he was present at meetings only the time it took him to do his duty and brief them, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the point. What is your point, Ms. Edgerton? So there is no point of asking this question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was consistent with what he had known about the Crisis Staff? I will allow the accused to continue his questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that you have answered this question?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any actions of the Crisis Staff contrary to this -- what we see here?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not while I was in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 31 in B/C/S. Can we now -- except for the brigade commander, who is hiding behind these titles, commander of the municipal staff, commander of the Kljuc defence command, et cetera? Can we know what this recording secretary meant with any certainty?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot know that. That's what I said before. When this meeting was held, five names were on the list for this post, and party people did not want me to be the town defence commander because I was not a member of the SDS, I was a member of the SK movement for Yugoslavia. However, the officer cadre got their way and they wanted me to be accepted, and they said an order would come down to establish the town defence and to appoint the commander. However, before that order came, which was never written, by the way, it would be in the documents otherwise - the order appointing the defence commander was never written, instead, a unit, the 17th Light Infantry Brigade was established, and beginning with 4th of June, I became assistant commander for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, and I stayed in that job until the end of the war and continued serving until 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it say about Bosko Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Bosko Lukic informed the Crisis Staff of the possibility of procuring certain technical equipment for the needs of a future light brigade which would probably be formed in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this what you have been talking about all this time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today, it was suggested to you that the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc took over the Muslim municipality of Kljuc and reinstated their territories and you said that it was carried out by a military body. Were there any military reasons for the military to do that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were military reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about that. What military reasons and justifications were there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The military justification was the fact that the Territorial Defence of Velagici had carried out an attack on the military convoy. They did what they did and the army reacted the way they did. I don't think that there is any military in the world that will allow others to kill the troops. And the military was the only body that carried out the attack, and arrested armed men who belonged to the unit and who carried automatic and semi-automatic rifles, mostly small arms in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now the last page. This was recorded on the 18th of June, 1992. It was another Crisis Staff meeting. It will probably be on page 38. Let's call up that page and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 20 of English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. The date is 18 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have it in Serbian. I'm going to read the text to you. It says here: "Marko Adamovic read the order of the brigade commander which the Crisis Staff accepted." What was your capacity when you were there and read out the order?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for moral guidance and religious and legal affairs. I was also assistant commander for information. My brigade commander sent me there to read that order, whatever that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was actually the only item on the agenda of that session. There was nothing else; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was e-court page 63 in B/C/S. Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Adamovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just with respect to P2606 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness can be excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. What we'll do is -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may be excused have a nice, safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. My apologies. I didn't mean to interrupt. With respect to P2606, what we'll do is try and take the pages out of the order in which they are presently uploaded and reload them in a coherent order and advise my colleague, Madam Registrar, and the Defence when that is done, in case we need to use it at any further point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At least we have the date correct so far. Yes. Is the next witness ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's Mikan Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Davidovic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such -- under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to make a pause after my question so that your words may be properly recorded. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9593 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the statement before you?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today here in the courtroom, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it also the Defence is tendering one associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zec, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives Exhibit D4166 and the associated exhibit, D4167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Davidovic's statement in English. [In English] Mikan Davidovic was born in Sanski Most municipality where he lived and worked throughout the course of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At present, he works at the Ministry of Administration and Local Self-Government in the government of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. Mikan Davidovic decided to join the SDS towards the end of 1991. The SDS was established as the party of the Serbian people in response to the establishment of the SDA and HDZ. The SDS was a democratic party with a decentralised structure. Mikan Davidovic was a member of the commission which organised the plebiscite in Sanski Most municipality. The plebiscite ensured after -- ensued after the Serbian members of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina were outvoted on the issue of the independence of BH whereby the Serbs thought that they should stay in Yugoslavia. Eventually, Muslims and Croats declared independence without Serbs. The SDS never adopted any policy of persecution, forcible deportation and ethnic cleansing. The population was relocated but that was due to fear of the conflicts that had broken out and the deterioration of the overall security situation in economic and social conditions. The SDS state bodies of Republika Srpska and Dr. Karadzic did not spread, instigate or enable a propaganda campaign among Bosnian Serbs with the intention of causing fear from and hatred against the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. In mid-June, 1992, Mr. Davidovic was appointed as the head of the department for professional and common affairs of Sanski Most municipality. During this period of time, he was not engaged in any of the SDS organs. In 1993, Mr. Davidovic was hired as the head of the centre for social welfare of Sanski Most municipality. The main activities of the institution concerned the most vulnerable population categories and, as part of these duties, the centre attempted to set up a register of citizens in need so that humanitarian aid would be distributed accordingly and in the fairest possible way. Among the needy, there were members of all ethnicities and attempts were made to ensure that all citizens irrespective of their ethnicity or religion had at least a bare minimum of life's necessities. Once the conditions of wide-ranging tensions and fear were created, non-Serbian population started moving out of -- out from Sanski Most. Mr. Davidovic was a member of the municipal commission for an unhindered departure which was set up to control the departure process, provide assistance and make sure that non-Serbs moved out from Sanski Most without any hindrance. The assistance requested by the citizens who wished to leave the municipality consisted of arranging contacts with competent institutions which made appropriate transportation arrangements, collecting the data from representatives of local communes and citizens from other ethnicities about the number of persons who expressed a wish to leave, announcing their departure to competent organs. Nobody had ever forced non-Serbs to move out. At first, people mostly moved within Bosnia and Herzegovina and then the number of requests to move abroad increased. That is why, at the end of 1993, a new commission was established and Mr. Davidovic became one of its members. The commission acted upon requests of those citizens who needed assistance with getting hold of their visas and helped them with group applications for approvals of their unhindered departure. The process was initiated and implemented by the representatives of non-Serbs. They performed all mediation tasks in relation to the take-over of the visas and established the place and time of entry into Croatia. And that is a short summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I would like to note that while paragraph 22 of this witness refers to adjudicated facts -- fact 2524, this adjudicated fact 2524 actually was not admitted in this case. Well, Mr. Davidovic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement about your role in the SDS and the municipal authorities in Sanski Most. Apart from this, Mr. Davidovic, you were also secretary of the Sanski Most municipal board and you attended sessions of the Serb Municipal Assembly and Executive Board; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, not all the time. I was not always present. Yes, I discharged the duties as the secretary, but I did not attend all the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out, you were assigned to the SJB police force; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never in the police, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25635.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this, you will see, Mr. Davidovic, is an overview of assignments in the SJB Sanski Most for June 1992. And if we can have second page --

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not me. This is another Mikan Davidovic, also from my village. I know the man, but that's not me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you look item number 34, it says Davidovic, Mikan, and this is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I know the guy. I'm sure that he's from my village. He is two years older than me, and he was indeed a member of the SJB or the MUP but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 17305.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a proposal for appointment sent to Mr. Karadzic in November 1996 -- 1994, excuse me. And on this page, can you see your name?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is me. This is a proposal for my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And here we see that you were proposed to the position of the chief of the SJB Sanski Most, at second page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that was indeed a proposal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we turn one more page in both languages? We need second page of the actual document which would be e-court 3. And here it says that you were proposed to this position by the SDS municipal board and the municipal Executive Board. This proposal was sent by Nedeljko Rasula and Mr. Rasula had been president of the Crisis Staff in 1992, and he remained to be a leading figure in Sanski Most in 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was also the president of the Municipal Assembly. When he sent this, he was the legally elected president of the municipality of Sanski Most. He was actually duty-bound. It was part of his duties to send this out to the competent institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's focus now to the work of the commission for relocation of population. You say in paragraph 20 that the first head of this commission was Bosko Banjac, but you did not provide any date. Bosko Banjac was assigned to this position in June 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the dates. It was a long time ago. I believe that it was in late 1992. The date may be correct, but I really can't remember it. I know for a fact that that was during the period when I arrived in Sanski Most and started working there. That was sometime in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P02732.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these are conclusions of the Crisis Staff from June 1992. At page 2, under item number 4, it says that Bosko Banjac is ordered to form a commission for population migration, consisting of five members. So you were a member of this commission headed by Banjac as of this date or shortly after; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not from this date but from a date much later. I can't remember the date. But the Executive Council set up the commission and I became its member, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So you don't remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the date. It was a long time ago. It was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 25636?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, are you saying that you were not in Sanski Most at this time or that you did not work in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was in the territory of Sanski Most but not in its urban part but in a village called Bosanski Milanovac which was some 15 to 20 kilometres away from the centre of the municipality. So I did not work in the municipality at the time. First, I was an intern and then I wasn't working anywhere. I was not employed either in Sanski Most proper or in the broader region of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And here you're looking at conclusions of the Crisis Staff from 16 June 1992. So can you read for us item number 6? What is the title?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: A commission is set up for the population. It is composed of -- what does it say here? Dusko Radic, Mirko Stanic, Sofija Praca-Veljovic, Mikan Davidovic, Borislav Stojicic. I never received this. Something has been crossed in this document. This commission never took off the ground. It never started operating. I don't know what these people did actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we not have English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It looks like it's in e-court but not released, I think. I can see the entry for translation but when I open it, it doesn't show any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Davidovic, I'm not sure -- you saying you were not working for municipality and then here Crisis Staff is basically ordering you to be a member of this commission for population. So you were in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. For instance, Sofija Praca-Veljovic, she was a professor working at the secondary school; Stanic Mirko, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about others. I'm asking about you. You were in Crisis Staff. You were ordered --

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff could order but I did not perform any functions. They did not inform me. I wasn't in the area. I wasn't available. Of course, the Crisis Staff could have placed me on any lists in any commission, and could have given me my purview and I would have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, it's not clear how Crisis Staff can order someone to do something that is not around. You were there. They appointed you to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that this commission did not carry out any activities and never took off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness in another case, in Brdjanin case, Besim Islamcevic, testified that in the period June or July 1992, you and Vlado Vrkes came to Podbrezje to explain people what categories of people can apply for papers necessary to leave Sanski Most. And he said again he met you in September 1992. These are transcript pages in Brdjanin case 7431, 7432, 7474. So witnesses saw you coming, talking to people about these issues, issues of immigration; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. At that time, I would come to the municipality, I met with SDS and the assembly of the municipality, and Vlado asked me to go to Podbrezje. I believe Islamcevic used to work in the football club. He was a coach there and I know him from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And he said you were in charge of immigration, it's not that you just happened to be there and going there with Vrkes but you were doing this sort of work.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was later. Yes, I did later on. After the Executive Council appointed that commission, this is what I did, and this is what I stated in my statement. This was towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And to be clear, Besim Islamcevic was talking about late June and after that, so it's not like sometimes later on, it's June 1992, you were dealing with resettlement of population called immigration.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was the period July, maybe even August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's move on. You say that Muslims and Croats left Sanski Most on their own desire. In fact, there were efforts throughout the Krajina region to force Muslims and Croats to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm your statement because I was not familiar with that. I do not have such information that you may have in your possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before I move on, I would like to tender this document and we will provide -- and we will provide translation shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, this Chamber has received evidence that the 1st Krajina Corps explicitly acknowledged that an attempt to expel Muslims and Croats failed because of the transportation difficulties and their resistance to leave their homes, P03664. So this was something that was taking place in Sanski Most among other municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These efforts in Sanski Most and elsewhere took the form of targeting Muslims and Croats, attacking and destroying their towns, places of residence and detaining many of them; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That fell within the purview of other organs. I was not competent for that and neither did I verify such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P03662.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is a combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps from May -- May 1992. We need page 2. At page 2, item number 3, it says that in areas of Prijedor, Kljuc and Sanski Most, mopping up continues. The resistance of Croat and Muslim formations is weak --

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is no Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So e-court page 3 in B/C/S, so it's page 2 of the actual document. So if you look at -- I was talking about item number 3. The resistance of Croat and Muslim formations is weak and their mass surrender is underway. A little bit below in item number 5(b), it says that after actions in Kozarac, Kljuc and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from the units, and the reasons they say was the massive destruction of their towns. So these were the reasons, Mr. Davidovic, massive destruction, people [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's possible but this is not known to me. It's possible but those facts were not known to me. What I did hear I heard it from people going there, that the problems were fear, so fear of combat activities, fear in terms of assistance, welfare assistance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You're repeating your statement. There is no need to do that. Your statement is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Just focus on the question and answer as short as you can. In the same paragraph here, it says that the situation was made worse by public statements made by the ARK SDS leaders who advocate moving and expelling all Muslims and Croats from these areas. So this -- these statements, Mr. Davidovic, caused the fear among non-Serb population and they wanted to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the same time, there were public announcements made over the radio to non-Serbs to surrender, otherwise they will be attacked and their homes and families devastated and destroyed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKAN DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not listen to radio. There were statements, there were information about the security situation, and the competent organs would issue them. But I do tell you really that I don't know much about that. I could not tell you with any degree of certainty what was broadcast on the radio at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm going to play to you what was broadcast on the radio in Sanski Most over and over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And can we have P00725. In the portion that I'm going to play is at -- on the transcript it's at page 7 of the English and page 11 and 12 of the B/C/S and it's a Sanski Most radio broadcast of 27 May 1992, and I'm going to play that -- a portion of it in court now and this portion is time code 15 minutes, 13 seconds, to 16 minutes 21 seconds of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, shall we stop. Two questions: Whether it's audible to the witness; second question, would you like to -- would you like the interpreters to interpret? We haven't heard any translation. First, Mr. Davidovic, can you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very poor sound, but there is some -- some portions are intelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have provided transcripts to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, shall we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn today I would like to issue one ruling. It's about the accused's request filed today in which he requested counsel for Vladimir Domazet be present during the proofing and testimony of Vidoje Blagojevic, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution indicated via e-mail that it did not wish to respond to the request. The Chamber takes no issue with Domazet's presence in the courtroom during Blagojevic's testimony. The request is therefore granted. The Chamber takes no position with regard to Domazet's presence during proofing. Mr. Davidovic, we will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you not discuss with anybody else about your testimony. The hearing is adjourned.
